query: Equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr exhibits 8–16% room-temperature tensile ductility in the cast state and a yield strength of 163–530 MPa at 1000 °C at strain rates of 10−4–10−2 s−1, but inadequate oxygen resistance prevents most practical high-temperature applications. Earlier oxidation-protection research prevented pesting in a related, non-equiatomic Hf–Nb–Ta–Ti–Zr alloy during a 5 h exposure to air at 800 °C, but that result does not establish protection for equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr; related studies on other refractory alloys likewise did not evaluate this composition. With preservation of useful room- and high-temperature mechanical performance as a design constraint, what single intervention could improve the oxygen resistance of equiatomic cast HfNbTaTiZr? Formulate one hypothesis identifying the intervention and mechanism, predicting the outcome relative to untreated material, defining the applicable temperature, atmosphere, exposure-time, and loading boundaries, citing supporting evidence from the prior studies, and specifying a controlled experiment and result that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Adding approximately 5 atomic percent Sn to equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr will form a protective, Sn-enriched oxide scale that suppresses pest oxidation without significantly degrading the room‐temperature ductility and high‐temperature yield strength of the cast alloy.
generation.material_initial_state: Equiatomic cast HfNbTaTiZr that shows 8–16% room-temperature tensile ductility and yield strengths of 163–530 MPa at 1000 °C but suffers from inadequate oxygen resistance (pesting) on exposure to air at high temperatures.
generation.intervention: Incorporate ~5 at.% Sn into the alloy composition during casting.
generation.conditions: Exposure to air at temperatures around 800 °C for durations up to 5 hours, where the alloy is not under significant mechanical stress.
generation.structural_mediator: Formation of a continuous, adherent Sn-enriched oxide (likely tin oxide) at the alloy surface.
generation.mechanism: The Sn addition is expected to segregate to the substrate–scale interface during high-temperature exposure, promoting the formation of a protective oxide that retards oxygen penetration and prevents the pesting phenomenon. This effect is analogous to prior results in similar refractory alloys where Sn improved scale adhesion and suppressed pest oxidation.
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared to the untreated equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr, the Sn-alloyed version should exhibit a significantly slower oxidation rate and reduced scale spallation during a 5-hour air exposure at 800 °C, while retaining comparable room-temperature ductility and high-temperature yield strength.
generation.baseline: The untreated equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr alloy that shows inadequate oxygen resistance (pesting) under similar high-temperature air exposure.
generation.boundary: Temperature limited to around 800 °C in air for exposures up to 5 hours; results may not extrapolate to more severe oxidation conditions or under significant mechanical load.
generation.uncertainty: The optimum Sn concentration and its possible influence on phase stability or minor effects on mechanical properties remain uncertain; additionally, scale composition and long-term adherence under cyclic conditions require further exploration.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two alloy batches: one cast from equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr and one with ~5 at.% Sn added. Subject both samples to air exposure at 800 °C for 5 hours in a furnace. Post-exposure, evaluate the oxide scale morphology via SEM, measure weight gains, and assess scale adhesion. In parallel, perform room-temperature tensile tests and high-temperature (≈1000 °C) yield strength measurements to compare the mechanical properties.
measurements: Oxide scale thickness and morphology (via scanning electron microscopy)
Weight gain (thermogravimetric analysis) as an index of oxidation rate
Adhesion and continuity of the scale (via cross-sectional imaging)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the Sn-alloyed alloy does not show at least a 20% reduction in oxidation kinetics or scale spallation compared to the untreated alloy, or if the mechanical properties are significantly degraded (e.g., >10% reduction in ductility or yield strength at high temperature), then the hypothesis that Sn addition improves oxygen resistance without deleterious effects is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: Structural metallic materials for applications at high temperatures must have a balance of mechanical properties and oxidation resistance. Coated and internally cooled Ni-based superalloys are used in gas turbine engines close to their high temperature limit, which is imposed by the melting temperature of Ni. The search for new alloys with similar or better capabilities at higher temperatures has concentrated on Nb-silicide based alloys that have lower densities, significantly higher solidus temperatures in excess of 1900 °C and can offer notable mechanical properties []. For example, some of these alloys can have compressive yield strength of about 1800 MPa at room temperature, 1200 MPa at 1000 °C and 500 MPa at 1200 °C []. The oxidation resistance of Nb-silicide based alloys was improved dramatically when the key alloying elements Al, Cr, Si, and Ti were in synergy with other transition and refractory metals, for example Hf, Mo, and simple metal and metalloid elements, e.g., Sn [,,,,]. In the case of Sn, the early research [,] concentrated on alloys where its concentration was low to avoid the formation of the A15-Nb3Sn compound. In 2007, Geng et al [] reported that the addition

Improvement of oxidation resistance at both temperatures was accompanied by a decrease and increase, respectively, of the alloy parameters VEC and δ, in agreement with the alloy design methodology NICE. Considering the questions that were presented in the introduction of the paper: a higher Sn concentration seems to be essential for suppressing the pest oxidation of Nb-24Ti-18Si based alloys with Cr and no Al additions, but not for alloys where Al and Cr are in synergy with Sn, the stability of Nb3Sn in the alloy is “assured” with 5 at.% Sn addition and does improve oxidation resistance with/out the presence of the Laves phase and the synergy of Sn with Al, both of which form A15 compounds and Al substitutes Si in Nb5Sn2Al, gives the “best” oxidation behaviour with improved scale adhesion at the high temperature.

The research on the oxidation of Nb-silicide-based alloys would suggest (a) that Ge and/or Sn are needed to suppress pest oxidation, and (b) that, when these alloying additions were present individually or simultaneously in the alloys, the spallation of their scales at high temperatures was not suppressed. It is now well established that Ge or Sn has an effect on macrosegregation and can also reduce the liquidus temperature of the alloy. Alloying with Sn can affect the stability of the Nbss but not the alloying with Ge, which can, however, significantly reduce the cracking of the substrate below the scale/substrate interface []. Unfortunately, from the oxidation research on multicomponent Nb-silicide-based alloys, it is not clear whether it was the synergy of Sn or Ge individually or simultaneously with Al, Cr, Si, and Ti that improved oxidation resistance, or whether the presence of oxygen scavenging Hf with/without transition and refractory metals and with some or all of the aforementioned elements was essential for increasing the oxidation resistance.

chosen.approach: Alloying addition (Sn/Ge/B) to form protective oxide scales
